title: A solvent-flux theory for nonequilibrium swelling dynamics of thermoresponsive microgels
authors: Arturo Moncho-Jordá, Alessandro Patti, Fabián A. García-Daza, Alejandro Cuetos
abstract: Thermoresponsive microgels undergo large reversible size changes as temperature alters solvent quality. Predicting their nonequilibrium swelling and deswelling kinetics is challenging because polymer volume fraction, mechanical response, and solvent transport evolve during large volume changes. Here we develop a solvent-flux theory for the dynamics of a spherical microgel. The radius-change rate is driven by the osmotic-pressure imbalance across the particle boundary and resisted by water transport through the polymer network, yielding a nonlinear equation for the global swelling coordinate and a state- and temperature-dependent swelling diffusion coefficient, $D_{\mathrm{SW}}(φ,T)$. In the linear-response regime, the theory recovers Tanaka--Fillmore exponential relaxation and the scaling $τ_\mathrm{SW}\sim R_{\mathrm{eq}}^2γ/K_{\mathrm{eq}}$, while providing a microscopic interpretation of the polymer--solvent friction coefficient $γ$. Beyond this limit, the model retains quadratic size scaling while accounting for state-dependent transport and mechanics. For pNIPAM microgels, it predicts asymmetric pathways, with deswelling faster than swelling over the same temperature interval. Finite thermalization produces a crossover from a microgel-controlled to a thermalization-controlled regime, in which the apparent relaxation time grows linearly with the external thermalization time and hysteresis-like loops emerge in the radius--temperature plane. A stochastic extension based on the Smoluchowski equation predicts transient broadening of the radius distribution during collapse, with maximal fluctuations in the volume-transition region. The theory links solvent transport, nonlinear swelling dynamics, thermalization effects, and nonequilibrium size fluctuations in responsive microgels.
summary: This paper introduces a solvent-flux theory to model the complex, non-equilibrium swelling and deswelling dynamics of thermoresponsive microgels. It derives a state-dependent mobility that governs the kinetics, predicting key non-linear behaviors such as asymmetric pathways and dynamic hysteresis. The work successfully links solvent transport, mechanical response, and size fluctuations in these soft matter systems.
main_problem: Predicting the nonequilibrium swelling and deswelling kinetics of thermoresponsive microgels, which is challenging due to the coupled evolution of polymer volume fraction, mechanical response, and solvent transport during large volume changes.
main_result: The theory predicts asymmetric swelling/deswelling pathways and shows that finite thermalization times can induce dynamic hysteresis-like loops in the radius-temperature plane.
method: Development of a solvent-flux theory that models the radius-change rate driven by osmotic-pressure imbalance and resisted by water transport through the polymer network.
model_or_system: The study focuses on thermoresponsive microgels, specifically pNIPAM, whose dynamics are governed by a nonlinear, state-dependent diffusion equation derived from solvent flux principles.
key_observables: Swelling diffusion coefficient ($D_{SW}(R, T)$), radius distribution width ($\sigma_R(t)$), and the rate of radius change ($dR/dt$).
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), polymer volume fraction ($\phi$), and the characteristic relaxation time ($	au_{SW}$).
main_assumptions: The theory assumes an overdamped, diffusion-controlled solvent transport regime and extends beyond the limitations of the linear-response Tanaka-Fillmore model.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the driving forces (osmotic pressure imbalance) for swelling and deswelling via solvent flux.
paper_structure: The paper develops the solvent-flux theory, derives the governing non-linear ODE for the swelling coordinate, analyzes the linear-response limit, and extends the model to include stochastic fluctuations and finite thermalization effects.
why_interesting: The framework of non-equilibrium dynamics, coupled transport, and fluctuating potentials is highly relevant to open quantum systems and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, providing a model for complex relaxation processes.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic illustration of the swelling of a pNIPAM microgel driven by solvent uptake. The inward solvent flux is induced by a positive osmotic-pressure imbalance, Π > 0, between the microgel interior and the surrounding bulk solu- tion,leading to an increase of the microgel radius. The oppo- site case, Π < 0, corresponds to deswelling, where solvent is expelled from the microgel and the particle radius decreases.

FIG. 2. (a) Equilibrium hydrodynamic microgel radius as a function of T. (b) Flory–Huggins solvency parameter as a function of T. Blue lines show the corresponding fits of Req(T) and χ(T) using Eqs. (36) and (37).

FIG. 3. (a) Normalized free-energy landscape of the microgel as a function of the particle radius R. (b) State-dependent swelling diffusion coefficient, DSW(R, Tf), as a function of R. In both panels, the black solid line corresponds to the deswelling process after a temperature jump to Tf = 321 K, whereas the red dashed line corresponds to the swelling pro- cess after a temperature jump to Tf = 288 K. Blue squares denote initial state, whereas blue triangles show the final equi- librium state.
FIG. 4. Instantaneous rate of change of the microgel radius, dR/dt, as a function of R for the deswelling process (black solid line) and the swelling process (red dashed line).

FIG. 5. (a) Time evolution of the microgel radius, R(t), dur- ing the deswelling and swelling processes. (b) Scaling of the characteristic relaxation time τ90 with the particle-size scal- ing factor α for both deswelling and swelling. The quantity τ90 is defined as the time required for the microgel radius to complete 90% of the total change between the initial and final equilibrium states.
